sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `_create_process_for_shard` is added but never invoked. WHY: Dead code indicates an incomplete restart design or a leftover helper from an earlier iteration; it may confuse future maintainers or mask the intended per-shard restart path. HOW: Either wire it into the restart logic where a single shard needs recovery, or remove it if the per-process restart model is the intended design.

WHAT: The shard tag key is 'shard' for spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes, but 'shards' for spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. WHY: Metrics pipelines aggregate by tag key, so the same shard dimension is split across two keys and dashboards will undercount or miss data. HOW: Use a single tag key such as 'shards' for all three metrics, since shard_tag is already a comma-joined list of shards.

issues.descricao: The wait_produce timer is tagged with 'shards' while sibling flusher metrics use 'shard' for the same value, so per-shard dashboards miss it.
issues.textoGolden: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

comentarios.texto: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with the key `"shards"`, while the other two metrics emitted in this same loop (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` at line 185 and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` at line 195) use the key `"shard"`. All three carry the same `shard_tag` value, so this is a pure key-name disagreement: any dashboard or alert that groups/filters by the `shard` tag will silently receive no data from `wait_produce`. Rename the tag key to `"shard"` so all flusher metrics share one tag.

The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `shards` while every sibling metric introduced/updated in the same method (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`) uses the singular key `shard`. Anything consuming this metric family by the `shard` tag (dashboards, alerts, tag-based aggregation) will silently receive no data for `wait_produce`, and per-shard breakdowns of produce latency will be incomplete. Change the tag to `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` so the tag contract matches the other flusher metrics.

The wait_produce timer tags with "shards", while the sibling metrics in the same loop use "shard" for the same value (shard_tag). Use one tag key, "shard", so queries and dashboards that group by it cover all of these metrics.

issues.descricao: The time.sleep(0.1) added to test_basic to let flusher threads process is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep.
issues.textoGolden: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The added synchronization point `time.sleep(0.1)` added after the second `step.poll()` is neutralized by the test's own `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 15 (same `time` module), so it does not actually wait. WHY: The comment says it 'Give[s] flusher threads time to process after drift change', but the call is a no-op, so the test still races the background flusher thread before `step.join()` and is liable to be flaky / to not exercise the intended post-drift flush path. HOW: Use a non-monkeypatched wait (e.g. capture the real sleep before patching, or use the flusher's thread/process join, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a real timeout).

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` does not wait: line 15 of the same test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `sleep` on the global `time` module, so this call (and the flusher's own `time.sleep`) is a no-op. The comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is therefore false — the call returns instantly and provides no synchronisation, so the test does not actually wait for the flusher to process after the drift change. Either synchronise on a real condition (e.g. wait until the expected message is produced) or, if the original `time.sleep` is needed here, patch a module-scoped reference instead of the global `time.sleep`.

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because the test patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so nothing waits for the flusher threads before `step.join()` and the `messages` assertion. Replace it with a condition-based wait, such as polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline. Use the real sleep saved before patching if a delay is needed.

issues.descricao: The restart path only kills a hung flusher if it is a multiprocessing.Process, but spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess, so hung processes are never killed and a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards.
issues.textoGolden: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

comentarios.texto: The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard does not match the SpawnProcess instances created by self.mp_context.Process. When a worker hangs, the guard skips kill() and the replacement starts while the original worker remains alive, allowing overlapping flushing of the same shards if the original resumes and leaking hung workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or self.mp_context.Process, and kill and join the old worker before replacing it.

The workers are created with get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances; these are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this guard skips kill() for actual production workers. When a worker hangs, the replacement starts while the original remains alive and can resume flushing the same shards. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the spawn-context Process class for the check, and fix the identical check in join() so shutdown also terminates surviving workers.

Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the separate multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently this guard skips kill() for production workers. When a live worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, the code starts a replacement and overwrites its handle while the original is still running. If the original resumes, both workers flush the same shards, and repeated hangs can exceed the configured process limit. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or explicitly distinguish threads) and stop the old worker before replacing it.

issues.descricao: join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping termination of the remaining flusher processes and leaving them running after shutdown.
issues.textoGolden: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

comentarios.texto: join() breaks out of the worker loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping cleanup for every remaining worker. If next_step.join consumes the timeout or an earlier worker exhausts it, remaining flushers can continue running after shutdown or partition reassignment. Use the deadline only to limit waiting and still terminate and reap every remaining process.

Do not break out of worker cleanup when the join deadline expires. If the first worker consumes the timeout, the next iteration breaks before terminating that worker or any subsequent workers. They may still be blocked in Redis or producer calls despite the shared stopped flag, leaving old workers running after strategy shutdown/reassignment. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of remaining time (using a type check that recognizes spawn-context workers).
join() waits for processes sequentially against a single shared deadline and breaks without terminating remaining processes once it expires, leaking them.

issues.descricao: The SpanFlusher docstring says it creates one process per shard, but shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

comentarios.texto: The docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the code at lines 60-66 shares shards across a capped number of processes (num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)); each shard assigned via i % self.num_processes). With the new --flusher-processes default of 1, a single process handles every shard, so the documented contract is the opposite of the behaviour this PR introduces (confirmed by test_flusher_processes_limit, which asserts 4 shards served by 2 processes). Update the docstring to say shards are distributed across up to max_processes flusher processes.

The new docstring says this creates one process per shard, but workers are capped by max_processes and shards are distributed among them. In particular, the CLI default of 1 means all assigned shards share one process. Describe capped workers with potentially multiple shards per worker so callers do not rely on per-shard process isolation.

The docstring says the flusher 'Creates one process per shard', but the number of processes is capped by max_processes (--flusher-processes), and shards are shared across processes via i % num_processes. Reword it to say that shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

issues.descricao: max_processes uses a truthiness fallback, so --flusher-processes 0 silently becomes one process per shard instead of being rejected.

comentarios.texto: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy value as 'not provided'. The new `--flusher-processes` click option is `type=int`, so a user can pass `0`; that legitimate-but-falsy value is discarded and the flusher silently spawns one process per shard instead of honoring the requested limit. Use an explicit None check, e.g. `self.max_processes = max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and validate/reject 0 upstream).

An explicit max_processes=0 is treated as an omitted limit by `or`, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` starts one process per assigned shard instead of respecting or rejecting the supplied zero limit. The CLI accepts zero as an integer and the factory forwards it unchanged. Default only when max_processes is None, and explicitly validate that supplied process limits are positive so zero cannot silently enable potentially many workers.

`max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'unset' and silently expands to one process per shard. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and reject values below 1.

issues.descricao: A negative --flusher-processes value is not validated and makes SpanFlusher construction fail with KeyError.

comentarios.texto: `flusher_processes` is not validated to be >= 1. `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` lets a negative value through (it is truthy), so `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` becomes negative and `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, leaving `process_to_shards_map` as `{}`. The following loop computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes`, which for any negative divisor is 0, so `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises KeyError and the consumer fails to construct. Since `flusher_processes` is exposed as an int CLI option (`--flusher-processes`), a negative value is reachable from configuration. Guard with `max(1, self.num_processes)` / validate the input.
negative max_processes flows through `or` guard into min() -> empty map -> KeyError on i % num_processes; empty assigned_shards yields zero processes.

issues.descricao: submit() queries cluster-wide Redis memory once per flusher buffer, repeating identical INFO calls per process on every submit.

comentarios.texto: The new loop calls get_memory_info() once per flusher buffer even though SpansBuffer.get_memory_info delegates to iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client), which fetches INFO for the entire Redis cluster regardless of assigned_shards. With P flusher processes and memory backpressure enabled, each submitted batch now performs P identical cluster-wide memory queries on the consumer thread instead of one, increasing Redis traffic and blocking ingestion. Fetch cluster memory information once from a single buffer.
submit() loop calls buffer.get_memory_info() per flusher but each call is cluster-wide from same client, repeating identical INFO N× per submit.

issues.descricao: _create_process_for_shard is added but never called.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is newly added but has no caller anywhere (grep for `_create_process_for_shard(` finds only its definition); the restart path actually used is `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. WHY: This is dead code that indicates the intended per-shard restart wiring was left incomplete — any future caller relying on restarting only the process owning a given shard will silently do nothing, and it is confusing which restart path is authoritative. HOW: Remove `_create_process_for_shard`, or wire it into `_ensure_processes_alive` if per-shard restart was intended.

issues.descricao: test_flusher_processes_limit counts assigned shards instead of checking that each shard is assigned exactly once.

comentarios.texto: The assertion counts shard entries rather than verifying shard assignment. A broken distribution such as {0: [0, 1], 1: [0, 1]} still passes all assertions in this test while shards 2 and 3 are never flushed. Assert that the flattened mapping contains exactly the expected assigned shards, with no duplicates (and verify each worker's shard buffer uses that mapping), rather than only asserting a total of four.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The working-hours guard rejects a slot when `workingHours.find` returns ANY same-day block the slot falls outside of, so a slot inside one availability block is wrongly rejected if the user also has a second block on the same weekday. WHY: Users with split working hours (e.g. 09:30-12:00 and 14:00-18:00 on the same day — a supported availability shape, and exactly what the test fixture defines) lose all slots that fall inside any earlier block, because the later block returns truthy from the predicate and triggers `return false`. HOW: only reject when the slot is outside EVERY same-day block, e.g. compute the same-day blocks first and return false only if none contain the slot.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check computes end from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, so slots that start within working hours but end after them are accepted.
issues.textoGolden: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — an exact duplicate of `start` — instead of using `slotEndTime`. WHY: the working-hours upper-bound test `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore compares the slot START against the working-day end, so a slot whose start is inside working hours but whose end (start + eventLength) overruns `workingHour.endTime` is never filtered and is reported as available, allowing bookings outside the host's working hours. HOW: compute `const end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute();`.

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`, so it always equals `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check is identical to the `start` check and never catches a slot that starts within working hours but ends past them. Use `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` for `end`.

`end` is computed identically to `start` (both from slotStartTime), so the check `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` can never reject a slot on the upper bound. A slot starting inside working hours but ending after workingHour.endTime is wrongly considered available; derive `end` from slotEndTime instead.

issues.descricao: The date-override check compares two dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, so zero-length (day off) overrides are never detected.
issues.textoGolden: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

comentarios.texto: This compares two separately constructed dayjs objects with `===` (reference equality), which is always false, so a zero-length override (start equal to end, whole day blocked) never returns true here. Compare timestamps, e.g. `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))`.

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separate dayjs object references, so `===` is always false. The zero-length date-override branch is dead code and such an override is never recognised as covering the day; compare values (e.g. .isSame() or .valueOf() === .valueOf()) instead.

The equality check compares two separately created Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, even when the override start and end represent the same instant. The intended zero-length/closed-day rejection is unreachable, and a slot beginning exactly at that instant can reach the dateOverrideExist success return. Compare timestamps or use isSame instead.

issues.descricao: When a date override exists for the day, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before checking busy times, so slots overlapping existing bookings are reported available.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: when `dateOverrideExist` is true the function returns `true` before running the `busy.every(...)` check at the end. WHY: on any day that has a matching date override, a slot inside the override is reported available without checking the host's existing bookings (`busy` is spread via `...schedule`/`...userSchedule`), so a fixed/loose host who already has a booking during the override window is still shown as free — enabling double-booking. HOW: do not return early here; fall through so the override branch only decides whether the slot is inside the override window, and let the existing `busy` evaluation decide availability (e.g. `if (dateOverrideExist) { /* within override, still check busy */ } else { /* fall through to busy */ }`).

The new `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` short-circuits the `busy` conflict check (and the workingHours check) for any slot that falls inside a date override window. Every caller of `checkIfIsAvailable` previously counted on it returning false for a slot that overlaps an existing booking; on days covered by a date override that guarantee is gone, so slots conflicting with the user's real bookings are now reported as available and can be double-booked. The override branch should let control fall through to the `busy.every(...)` check (returning true only for the availability-window part) instead of returning early.

A matching date override returns true before checking busy periods. Both fixed-host and loose-host callers pass calendar and booking conflicts in busy, so a host with an override is offered even when an existing booking overlaps the slot. Continue to the busy checks after validating the override instead of returning true.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check rejects a slot when any interval for the weekday excludes it, so split schedules (e.g. morning and afternoon) reject all slots.

comentarios.texto: The working-hours predicate rejects a slot if any interval on its weekday does not contain it. A split schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 therefore loses every slot, since each valid slot lies outside the other interval. Require at least one matching interval to contain the full event instead of finding an interval that excludes it.

This search rejects a slot if it falls outside any working-hours window on that weekday. With split hours of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a valid 10:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the afternoon window. Check for containment in at least one applicable window rather than finding any window that excludes the slot.

WHAT: Outside-working-hours test uses workingHours.find() returning true if ANY entry rejects the slot. WHY: With split schedules (two entries same weekday, e.g. morning+afternoon) a valid morning slot is outside the afternoon entry, find() matches and the slot is wrongly rejected as outside hours. HOW: Invert logic to accept if ANY entry contains the slot (e.g. !workingHours.some(entry contains slot) => outside).

issues.descricao: The date-override bound compares the slot start, not the slot end, with the override end, so slots extending past the override are accepted.

comentarios.texto: The override bounds reject only non-overlapping slots rather than requiring the entire event to fit inside an override. A fixed host with a 10:00–11:00 override accepts a 10:30–11:30 event generated from another host's availability, despite being unavailable for its final half hour. Accept only when at least one override contains both slotStartTime and slotEndTime; this also avoids rejecting a slot merely because another interval on the same date does not overlap it.

The upper bound checks whether slotStartTime is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override end but finishes after it is treated as available. Compare slotEndTime with the override end using isAfter, so the slot must fit entirely inside the override.

issues.descricao: The override timezone conversion keeps only hour and minute, so overrides that cross midnight in the invitee timezone become inverted ranges or are applied to the wrong day.

comentarios.texto: Timezone conversion takes only hour and minute, discarding day rollover and turning intervals crossing attendee midnight into reversed ranges. A UTC organizer's 22:00–23:00 override viewed in UTC+01:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30, which buildSlots skips because start is greater than end, removing valid availability. Preserve the converted dates and split the interval across attendee-day boundaries before building slots.

WHAT: activeOverrides are filtered by UTC day (line 206-207) before the invitee/organizer offset is applied (lines 212-224), and shifted hours are not re-bucketed across midnight. WHY: An override that shifts to the previous/next calendar day in the invitee timezone is dropped from the wrong day or applied to the wrong day, so slots show open when the organizer is off (and vice versa). HOW: Filter/bucket overrides in the invitee-local date after applying the offset, or emit split entries spanning two invitee days.

issues.descricao: The new working-hours check does not reject slots on weekdays that have no working-hours entry, so those slots are treated as available.

comentarios.texto: A weekday with no matching working-hours entry falls through to the busy checks and is treated as available when there are no conflicts. In round-robin events, slots generated for a loose host can consequently include a fixed host whose schedule excludes that day. Reject slots unless a working-hours interval on the slot's weekday contains the event, when no date override applies.

issues.descricao: checkIfIsAvailable's date-override check never rejects a slot that starts before the override start (only one that ends before it), so slots partly outside the override hours are treated as available.

The override day is computed with local-time dayjs(date.start) while the slot day is formatted in UTC, so on a server not running in UTC overrides near midnight are applied to the wrong day or skipped.
With several date-override ranges on the same day, a slot is rejected as soon as it falls outside any one of them, so slots inside the other ranges become unavailable.

sugestoes.texto: The default value for `queued` is evaluated at import time because it's a time-dependent expression. It should be a factory to be evaluated per instance. Currently `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is shared across all instances, leading to incorrect timestamps if the default is used. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

issues.descricao: AssignmentSource.queued defaults to timezone.now() evaluated at class definition, so all instances share the import-time timestamp instead of the time they were queued.
issues.textoGolden: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates once at class-definition time so every AssignmentSource without explicit queued shares the same timestamp. WHY: queued time is wrong/stale for all later instances and defeats its purpose as a queue-time marker. HOW: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `field` import).

Field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import so all AssignmentSources share the same timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance measures its actual creation/queue time.

The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value (which is exactly what `from_integration` does, and what `from_dict` falls back to when the key is absent) shares the same frozen import-time timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was actually queued. This makes the `queued` timestamp semantically wrong/meaningless (it reflects process start, not assignment time) and would silently misreport the queue time anywhere this value is later inspected. Fix by defaulting in a factory/`__post_init__` or making the caller pass the timestamp, e.g. set `queued` inside `from_integration` (`queued=timezone.now()`), or use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Narrowing the cache lock to only `b.cache[key] = idx` makes cache entries observable in the middle of a build, so two concurrent builds for the same `NamespacedResource` can run simultaneously and the later one overwrites the first. WHY: A reader that already fetched the first index keeps using it after `b.cache[key]` is reassigned, so subsequent writes/deletes handled by the second index are silently ignored by that reader (and both builders create/overwrite the same on-disk directory under `b.opts.Root`). HOW: Before building, re-check `b.cache[key]` under `b.cacheMu` and return the existing index, or keep a per-key in-flight lock (e.g. keyed singleflight) so only one build per key is in flight while still allowing builds for different keys to proceed in parallel.

issues.descricao: BuildIndex now locks only the final cache assignment, so concurrent callers for the same uncached key all build the same expensive index in parallel and the last one overwrites the others.
issues.textoGolden: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Removing the function-wide `b.cacheMu.Lock()/defer Unlock()` and keeping only the lock around `b.cache[key]=idx` removes the only thing that serialized GetIndex against an in-flight build. WHY: getOrCreateIndex (resource/search.go:287-307) does GetIndex -> if nil -> build; previously BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole body so a concurrent caller's GetIndex (RLock) blocked until the first build cached the index and then saw it (no second build). Now GetIndex can return nil while a build for the same key is still running, so two requests/watch events build the SAME key concurrently — producing two distinct index instances where the caller holding the non-cached one never observes later writes (stale search results), and, for file-backed indices (size > FileThreshold), two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opening the same on-disk directory. HOW: guard the build per key (e.g. re-check the cache under the write lock after acquiring it, or use a per-key single-flight/lock so only one build runs per NamespacedResource), rather than relying on a global write lock held for the entire body.

The cache mutex was moved to cover only the cache assignment, removing the serialization that previously surrounded the whole BuildIndex. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can now both construct an index (including `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same on-disk path) and both write `b.cache[key]`; the second overwrites the first, so callers get distinct index instances for one key and writes made through the losing instance are invisible to readers of the cached one (and the file-backed build may collide on the same directory). Keep the build for a given key serialized (e.g. restore the lock around the build, or take a per-key lock) instead of locking only the map write.

Locking only cache publication allows concurrent requests for the same uncached key to build separate indexes and overwrite each other's cache entries. Search and handleEvent both call getOrCreateIndex, whose GetIndex previously blocked behind the build-wide lock; now an event can update one newly built index before another build replaces it, losing that update from subsequent search results and leaving the discarded index open. Serialize builds per NamespacedResource and recheck the cache after acquiring that per-key guard.

comentarios.texto: The newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call is unsafe: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-150) iterates `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`, while the bleve.go hunk in this same PR keeps `cacheMu` for the `b.cache[key] = idx` write only. Because search.go:207-213 already started the watch-event goroutine that can call `build` → `BuildIndex` → cache write, line 216 can iterate the map concurrently with that write, causing a `concurrent map iteration and map write` panic or data race. A write event for an unindexed resource can concurrently publish an index through BuildIndex, causing a map iteration/write race and potentially a fatal runtime error during initialization. Protect TotalDocs cache iteration with the same read lock used by GetIndex.

issues.descricao: BlockedEmail.should_block? updates match_count and last_match_at as a side effect of email validation, so each signup attempt (validated twice) inflates the counter and concurrent updates can lose increments.
issues.textoGolden: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: should_block? mutates match_count/last_match_at via read-modify-write save inside a validator. WHY: Every validation call (including re-validations of the same attempt or attempts failing on unrelated fields like username) inflates stats, and concurrent signups lose increments with no atomic update. HOW: Move stats update out of validation or use atomic increment (update_counters/increment_counter) only on actual blocked rejections.

WHAT: `should_block?` mutates state (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, calls `record.save`) inside a method that is invoked from the model validation callback, and the signup controller runs validation twice per attempt (`user.valid?` at users_controller.rb:168 then `user.save` at :172). WHY: a single signup attempt increments `match_count` twice and rewrites `last_match_at`, so the per-email block statistics the feature was built to track are wrong. HOW: make the read side non-mutating for validation and record the match separately (e.g. move the increment out of validation, or guard it so it runs once per attempt), keeping the predicate pure.

WHAT: `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write with no lock or unique constraint protection. WHY: two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can both read the same `match_count` and one write overwrites the other, losing counts, so the tracked statistics drift under load. HOW: use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or a database-level counter increment.

issues.descricao: Claims the 'returns false' spec cannot distinguish nil from false because be_false is a truthiness matcher.

comentarios.texto: This test is named "returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist," but it cannot verify that. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, which yields `nil` (not `false`) when no record exists, and under this suite's RSpec 2 semantics `subject.should be_false` is a truthiness matcher that passes for any falsy value including `nil`. The assertion therefore passes on the nil the code actually returns and would only fail on an outright `true`; it does not pin the `false`/`nil` distinction its name asserts. Assert the value exactly (e.g. `subject.should == false`, or `be_falsey`/`be_nil` if nil is intended) so a regression returning a non-false falsy value is caught.

issues.descricao: The domain whitelist/blacklist regex @(domains) is not anchored at the end, so an address like user@example.com.evil.com matches a whitelist entry for example.com and bypasses the restriction.
issues.textoGolden: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: email_in_restriction_setting? builds unanchored Regexp "@(domains)" with only '.' escaped. WHY: Whitelist 'gmail.com' substring-matches 'victim@gmail.com.evil.com', so an attacker registers with an unapproved domain and bypasses the allow-list; blacklist similarly over/under-matches and other regex metachars are unescaped. HOW: Anchor and escape domains (e.g. Regexp.escape per domain split on '|' plus /\A[^@\s]+@(?:domain)\z/i).

issues.descricao: Emails rejected by the server are cached in rejectedEmails for the controller's lifetime and never cleared, so an address that later becomes valid keeps failing client-side validation until reload.
A spec comment says last_match_at shows whether an email has ever been blocked, but should_block? updates it on every match, including do_nothing records.

sugestoes.texto: With 50 members and limit 50, the UI shows `1/2` and `next` moves offset to `user_count`, which loads an empty member list. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` instead.

issues.descricao: The admin group pager computes total pages as floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so when the member count is an exact multiple of the limit it shows an extra page and Next navigates to an empty member list.
issues.textoGolden: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

comentarios.texto: totalPages (and currentPage) use `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which is an off-by-one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 members, limit 50 → reports 2 pages although only 1 exists). This leaves `showingLast` false on the real last page, so 'next' navigates to an empty page at offset=user_count. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (and compute currentPage consistently) to get the correct page count.

totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives 2 for user_count=50, limit=50, although 50 members occupy exactly one page. Correct it to `Math.ceil(this.get('user_count') / this.get('limit'))`. Effect: for a group whose member count is a multiple of the page size, totalPages is one too high, showingLast remains false so the 'next' link stays enabled, and clicking it navigates to a phantom empty page.

`totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which over-counts by one whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with limit 50 yields 2 pages instead of 1). Since `showingLast` is `propertyEqual("currentPage", "totalPages")`, on a full last page `showingLast` is false, so the `next` action stays enabled and advances `offset` to `user_count`, rendering an empty page labeled as the last page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the zero-member guard) so the count matches the real number of pages.

issues.descricao: Several Group model functions (findMembers, destroy, userCountDisplay) return a value on some paths and undefined on others, triggering consistent-return lint warnings.

issues.descricao: Paging actions fire overlapping member requests and each response unconditionally overwrites offset and members, so a stale response arriving last can revert the list to an earlier page.

comentarios.texto: Guard against stale member-fetch responses before updating the model. `next` updates offset immediately and leaves navigation enabled, so with at least three pages two rapid clicks issue requests for offsets 50 and 100. If the offset-100 response arrives first and the offset-50 response arrives last, this unconditional `setProperties` resets both offset and members to the older page, undoing the latest navigation. Refreshes after membership changes can similarly be overwritten by an earlier fetch. Track a per-model request generation and apply only the latest response, or serialize navigation and refresh requests.

issues.descricao: The public members endpoint now always caps results at 50 per page, but the public group members page has no pagination, so groups with more than 50 members are silently truncated for users.

comentarios.texto: The public members route now loads only the model's default 50-member page without providing any way to request subsequent pages. The public group/members.hbs template only renders members and has no Next/Previous controls, so members after the first 50 become inaccessible (manual groups previously returned all members). Add public pagination controls and actions that update offset and reload members.

The new default limit applies to nonautomatic groups as well, but the public group-members route still calls findMembers() only once and its template simply iterates members without pagination. Previously this endpoint returned every member of a nonautomatic group; now a group with more than 50 members exposes only the first 50 on its public members page, with no way to reach the rest. Update that consumer to fetch subsequent pages or provide pagination when introducing this endpoint contract.

Provide pagination or load subsequent pages for the public group-members view. findMembers now requests only 50 members, and this route calls it only once while its template simply iterates members without navigation. Custom groups previously returned all members, so groups larger than 50 now have members that cannot be viewed on this page.

issues.descricao: Creating a group ignores the alias_level the admin selected, saving only name and visibility, so new groups keep the default alias level.

comentarios.texto: Persist params[:alias_level] when creating a group, just as update does. The creation form exposes aliasLevelOptions and group.asJSON sends the selected alias_level, but create saves only name and visible. A newly created group therefore retains the default alias level instead of the administrator's selection.

issues.descricao: Removing a member deletes the membership row directly and skips clearing the user's primary_group_id, so a removed user can keep this group as their primary group.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: remove_member uses group.users.delete(user_id) instead of the Group#remove destroy path. WHY: bypasses GroupUser destroy callbacks and primary_group_id cleanup done in destroy_deletions, leaving stale membership side-effects (e.g. dangling primary_group_id). HOW: load the User and call group.remove(user).

Removing a member with group.users.delete bypasses the primary_group_id cleanup previously performed by Group#destroy_deletions during usernames updates. A user whose primary group is this group remains associated with it as their primary group after membership removal, leaving stale primary-group state used by user administration and post serialization. Clear primary_group_id for the removed user when it equals this group's id as part of the removal operation.

issues.descricao: The remove_member spec issues a PUT request although the route only maps DELETE to remove_member, so the test uses a verb never routed in production.
issues.textoGolden: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

comentarios.texto: This example sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the PR maps `remove_member` only to DELETE (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`); PUT on that path routes to `groups#add_members`. Controller specs bypass the router, so the example still lands on `remove_member` and passes regardless — it would still pass if the DELETE route were missing or wired to the wrong action, leaving the newly introduced verb/action pairing untested. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member`, as the sibling example at line 125 already does.

The test 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the route is `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`. It exercises the action with a verb that is never routed in production. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` so the test matches the real request.

issues.descricao: Admin add_members pushes every username into group.users without skipping existing members, so adding someone already in the group hits the unique group_users index, returns a 500 and leaves earlier users partially added.
The public group members endpoint takes `limit` from params with no upper bound or positivity check, letting a visitor request huge pages or trigger a 500 with a negative limit.
Admin remove_member calls group.users.delete with a raw integer id, which raises RecordNotFound (404/500) when the user is not or no longer a member, e.g. on concurrent removal.
Admin remove_member deletes memberships with group.users.delete, which skips GroupUser callbacks, so the cached groups.user_count is never decremented and stays inflated.
Group member pagination is off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit: Next moves to offset == user_count and shows an empty page.
`add_members` runs one User query per username; load all users with a single `User.where(username: ...)` query.

sugestoes.texto: Lowering the redirect loop bound from 10000 to 1000 means segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects stop resolving to the real segment root. Their spans land in a different set and get flushed as separate segments. The change is unrelated to eviction; restore the previous bound or make it configurable.

issues.descricao: ZUNIONSTORE merges sorted sets with the default SUM aggregate, so a span payload present in both keys gets a doubled end-timestamp score and is wrongly kept by the oldest-first eviction.

comentarios.texto: ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so when the same span payload is present in both `set_key` and the merged `span_key`/`parent_key` (duplicate delivery is anticipated by this buffer's own comments), its score is added instead of being kept equal to `end_timestamp_precise`. Because eviction at line 63 (`zpopmin` by score) compares scores across all members of `set_key`, a summed score makes the duplicated span appear far newer than its real end timestamp and biases eviction away from legitimately-old spans, breaking the stated 'evict oldest end timestamps' contract. Use ZUNIONSTORE ... AGGREGATE MIN (or MAX) so a duplicate keeps a single end timestamp score rather than doubling it.

ZUNIONSTORE uses its default SUM aggregation, so replayed payloads present in both the temporary parent_key and the resolved set_key receive the sum of their end timestamps. Replaying a child whose parent already redirects to an ancestor therefore makes that old span score roughly twice its actual timestamp, protecting it from eviction over genuinely newer spans. Use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN for identical timestamp scores) on both union operations to preserve timestamp scores when members overlap.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both the destination and source has its timestamp doubled rather than preserved. This can happen when a previously merged span is replayed into its original subtree key. The duplicated span then sorts after genuinely newer spans and survives ZPOPMIN eviction incorrectly. Specify AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, since identical payloads should have identical timestamps) on both union calls so merging remains idempotent and scores remain end timestamps.

issues.descricao: Segment keys change from Redis sets to sorted sets under the same key names, so keys left by the previous release make ZADD, ZCARD and ZSCAN fail with WRONGTYPE during rollout, crashing span processing and flushing.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Changed SET ops (scard/sunionstore) to ZSET ops (zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin) with no migration breaks in-flight segments. WHY: Old keys of type SET still live up to TTL; ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN/ZADD on the opposite type raises WRONGTYPE and fails inserts/flushes during rollout.

The segment keys were migrated from Redis SETs to SORTED SETs (ZADD/ZSCAN/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN), but nothing handles the keys written by the currently deployed release. During a rolling deploy, an existing `span-buf:s:{...}:{id}` key is still a SET, so this `p.zadd(...)` (and the flusher's `p.zscan(...)`, and the Lua `zcard`/`zunionstore`) raises WRONGTYPE 'Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value'. That exception is unhandled: it aborts the whole pipeline/Lua invocation and crashes the consumer batch. Add a key-schema version to the key name (or a migration/fallback) so old SET-typed keys cannot be touched as sorted sets.

The new ZADD writes sorted sets into the same span-buf:s namespace previously populated by SADD, without migrating existing set keys. During deployment, inserting into an existing buffered segment fails with WRONGTYPE, and the new ZSCAN reader likewise fails on pending old-format segments instead of flushing them. Introduce a coordinated migration/drain or a versioned namespace with compatible handling of pending old-format buffers.

issues.descricao: Claims zpopmin eviction can drop the root span while the has-root flag stays set, flushing a segment without its root.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: zpopmin eviction by lowest end_timestamp has no protection for the segment/root span. WHY: Root with smallest or tied timestamp (tests use identical timestamps, ties break lexicographically) is evicted while hrs flag stays 1, flushing a root-marked segment missing its root.

issues.descricao: max_segment_spans is still a constructor parameter but is no longer enforced; the segment cap is now hardcoded to 1000 in the Lua script, so the configured value is ignored.

comentarios.texto: This hunk removes the only load-time span-count cap (`self.max_segment_spans`): previously a segment exceeding 1001 spans was logged, deleted from `payloads`/`cursors`, and skipped, but now every scanned span is unconditionally appended via `payloads[key].extend(...)`. The new bound relies entirely on insert-time eviction in the Lua script; if that eviction fails to bound a key (e.g. duplicated/scored members or the concurrent-writer case the code itself warns about at lines 457-461), this method will now materialize an unbounded number of spans into memory and emit them, whereas before it was safely skipped. Re-introduce a span-count guard (or verify the invite-time eviction strictly caps cardinality) to keep memory bounded.

buffer.py declares the segment span limit as the configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001, line 150) and this hunk removed the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` size guard from the flush path, while the other changed file (add-buffer.lua line 62) now enforces a hardcoded cap of 1000 spans. The two changed files disagree on what the segment span limit is: the Lua cap (1000) is not the declared `max_segment_spans`, and the buffer no longer applies the declared limit at all. If `max_segment_spans` is configured below 1000 (or below the Lua cap), oversized segments that this code used to skip will now be flushed. Reconcile the constant: either keep/restore the buffer-side guard against `self.max_segment_spans`, or make the Lua cap derive from the same limit instead of hardcoding 1000.

The segment size cap is hardcoded as 1000 here, but SpansBuffer still declares max_segment_spans = 1001 in src/sentry/spans/buffer.py, and this PR deleted the flush-time guard that used that constant. The declared limit and the actually-enforced limit now disagree (and the Python constant is no longer honored anywhere). Make the Lua cap and the Python constant agree — either pass max_segment_spans in as an ARGV instead of the literal 1000, or update the declared constant to 1000 — so the buffer's enforced bound matches the value it declares.

issues.descricao: Tests give every span the same end timestamp and never exceed 1000 spans, so the new score ordering and oldest-first eviction are not tested.

comentarios.texto: All spans in the fixture use identical end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so the ZSET score-dependent behavior (ordering by end time, zunionstore score merge, and Lua zpopmin keeping newest 1000) is neutralised — tests pass even if scores are wrong or eviction keeps the wrong end. Use distinct timestamps and add a >1000-span trimming test asserting oldest evicted.
The missing test for the new trim path (zset ordering/trim by end_timestamp_precise, the >1000-span zpopmin path) is a coverage gap. Add a test that verifies the new trim behavior.

issues.descricao: The span redirect-walk limit was cut from 10000 to 1000 iterations, so trees deeper than 1000 may not resolve to the correct segment root.
The spans buffer module docstring still describes span-buf:s:* keys as plain sets, though they are now sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise and trimmed to 1000 spans by add-buffer.lua.
The set_key variable name no longer matches the sorted-set data type after the switch to zadd/zscan.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `should_block?` increments `match_count` as a non-atomic read-modify-write, and it runs inside a validator. WHY: `UsersController#create` can validate twice (`user.valid?` and then `user.save`), so one signup attempt can be counted twice. Concurrent attempts can also lose updates. HOW: Use an atomic `update_all`/`increment_counter`, and avoid recording stats from within validation, or record them only once per attempt.

issues.descricao: When the server rejects an email, the signup form marks it with the generic 'invalid email' text instead of the server's reason (blocked or not allowed).

comentarios.texto: The message shown for a rejected email disagrees with the reason the code is reacting to. This branch fires when the server rejected the email (result.errors.email), and this PR gives that condition its own server string — user.email.blocked, added in config/locales/server.en.yml as "is not allowed." — but the client re-labels it with the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid'). A user whose address is perfectly well-formed but blocked/hosted on a blacklisted domain is therefore told their email is invalid, contradicting the reason just returned by the server. Use the blocked/not-allowed message (and add a matching client locale key) instead of user.email.invalid. Notice the same generic string is used at line ~94 for validation failures, so it should not be reused to represent a distinct server-side rejection.

issues.descricao: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the email with a case-sensitive exact match and no normalisation, so changing the letter case of a blocked address bypasses the block list.
issues.textoGolden: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

comentarios.texto: Blocked-email lookup compares the raw email without normalizing its domain. A signup for block@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG does not match a blocked record for block@spamfromhome.org despite identifying the same mailbox, allowing the signup restriction to be bypassed by changing domain capitalization. Normalize domains using Email.downcase both when storing blocked emails and when looking them up.

Canonicalize blocked emails consistently with the application's Email.downcase identity handling, both when storing entries and when looking them up. This exact equality query is case-sensitive, and BlockedEmail's validation callback only defaults action_type. A block-list entry such as `Block@SpamFromHome.org` therefore does not block the same identity submitted/stored as `block@spamfromhome.org`. This is particularly relevant to the explicitly supported manually populated block list. Normalize existing/imported entries as well as new ones, and add a test with differing casing between the stored entry and the lookup.
Case-sensitivity bypass: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) is exact case-sensitive with no normalization, while sibling checks are case-insensitive. Normalize (downcase/strip) on write and lookup.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS syntax. WHY: on GNU sed (Linux) the empty string is read as a filename, so the command fails and `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` is not updated, even though the script then prints a success message. HOW: use a portable form such as `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"`.

issues.descricao: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId with an empty data object, so Prisma does not refresh the @updatedAt timestamp and SelectedCalendar.updatedAt never reflects the cache refresh.
issues.textoGolden: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data {} to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. WHY: Prisma updateMany rejects empty data (validation error) or no-ops without touching @updatedAt, so the refresh path throws or silently leaves updatedAt stale. HOW: pass an explicit touch field e.g. { updatedAt: new Date() }.

Comment claims "Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt" but call passes empty object {} as data, so nothing is updated (Prisma updateMany with empty data is a no-op/error). Fix comment or pass { updatedAt: new Date() } to match the stated intent.

updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data {}. Prisma updateMany throws when data is empty, so this line throws on every resync after the cache write. Pass an explicit touch e.g. { updatedAt: new Date() } instead of {}.

issues.descricao: After deleting the calendar cache, CredentialActionsDropdown does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, so where no parent refetch callback is passed the stale cache status and delete action remain visible.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `deleteCacheMutation`'s `onSuccess` only calls `onSuccess?.()` and never invalidates the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query, while the sibling `disconnectMutation` explicitly invalidates it in `onSettled`. WHY: the 'Cache Status' row in the dropdown is rendered from the cached `connectedCalendars` result; after deleting the cache the query is not refetched, so the deleted status/last-updated entry stays visible and stale in the UI. HOW: invalidate the query in the cache-deletion mutation as well, e.g. `const utils = trpc.useUtils(); onSuccess: async () => { ...; await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate(); }`.

WHAT: deleteCacheMutation onSuccess only calls onSuccess?.() and never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, unlike disconnectMutation onSettled. WHY: cacheUpdatedAt stays stale after deletion so UI keeps showing old Last updated and delete action until manual refetch. HOW: add onSettled invalidate of connectedCalendars like disconnect does.

Successful cache deletion does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt. The wrapper forwards only an optional parent onChanged callback and disables window-focus refetch, so the deleted cache continues to appear present with its old timestamp and delete action. Invalidate utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars on successful deletion.

issues.descricao: The cache 'last updated' timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded en-US locale instead of the user's locale, so non-US users see US-style dates in an otherwise translated label.
issues.textoGolden: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

comentarios.texto: The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded "en-US" locale (new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)), so every user — regardless of their locale — sees a US-style date/time while the surrounding label is translated. Use the app's locale-aware date formatting helper (the user's current locale) instead of pinning en-US.

Date format hard-coded to "en-US" via Intl.DateTimeFormat while surrounding strings use t()/useLocale. Users in other locales see US short date/time. Use the active locale from useLocale/i18n instead of hard-coding "en-US".

The cache timestamp is always formatted with "en-US", even though the surrounding label uses the user's selected translation locale.
